item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Friday.
item.description:
Four guys
in the elevator, lamenting the news. For three of them, he was the Professor. For me, he was the Captain.
I shouldâve made the case for Sejanus as well, since thatâs where I first saw him. I was working the Northrup King Seed company summer route down south, and on Friday I would try to get the nearest PBS station on the motel TV and watch âI, Claudius.â Local beer on ice in the sink, Roman betrayal on the black-and-white. He was perfect - arrogant, dissembling, flashing a false smile, scheming, and - spoiler - dying on the steps from wounds he most surely deserved. That was forty-six years ago. Still remember his performance.
More on the matter on Tuesday, for reasons you will immediately understand. Part of a larger matter.
BTW, I saw the announcement on X, and I knew exactly what it meant, but I denied what I was seeing. I thought that Patrick Stewart was telling us to donate to Alzheimerâs research. Itdidnât seem plausible that he had it, let alone had died from it - he was old, yes, but vigorous. But like I say, I know exactly what it meant when I saw it, and I refused to believe it. Went to the page I used for general news. Sagged and sighed.
Back to the old neighborhood
today for another dog prescription. The usual irritation and disbelief. I mean, that's the strange emotion I get when I'm back:
disbelief I can't go home.
Otherwise, a carbon-copy day, proceeding through all the basics. Morning website work, write the Substack, post, lunch, dog walk to find the new poop place since everything's ripped up. Gym. In the locker room a very tall and heavy-set late-30s guy with black greasy hair said HELLO, and I said, hey. He asked about Halloween decorations in the neighborhood, and whether I'd put up any. I said I had not. He said, with a rather flat aspect, "no guts, no rotting torsos, no skeletons," and I said noooo, not in my part of Edina.
He wanted to know if there was a haunted house in Edina. A place where you go and, you know, it's full of Halloween. Did I know if there were any. I shrugged, trying not to look at the odd tattoo of bones and a eusophogus on his throat, and said he might try google, I don't know. I wasn't much of a Halloween guy myself.
Not a Halloween guy,
he said, looking away. I figured that was my daily human interaction, not counting chatting with the front desk staff at the gym, but no, someone waved to me as I was walking Birch through the Promenade. I had no idea who he was; he shouted I LIVE AT THE FRED so I walked over to see who, and said a few things, and he tapped on his headphones and said "I'm on a phone call," so I waved and let him go.
Everything's going to be odd today, then.
Off to Target to drop off the scripts for Birch, and what's this? The staff is completely different. The very large pharmacist with the wig of rainbow hair and the upside-down crosses painted on the cheek is gone, and the head pharmacist, who has a heavy accent and always wears a mask and is thus somewhat difficult to understand, is gone. In their place are bright cheerful people who smiled and spoke with crisp clarity.
Everything
is
odd today.
It's the end of the month,
and you know what that means: our round-up of Cheap Chinese Crap Products, or CCCP. I've been looking for new slippers, and of course there's a brand that is also a LIFESTYLE
Which day? The day where he takes the kid back to the salon to do something about those hideous braids?
Why is it great? Because slippers. Slippers that began with an idea, namely,
what if we sold slippers? And what if dogs were involved?
I am not sure what is going on here, taxonomy-wise:
No indication yet this was all ginned up by Chinese AI, but -
Ah.
One of the quirks
of the miserable chum ads: they have nothing to do with Costco, but invoke the brand all the time. In this case, it's a portable device for compressing clothes so you can get more in the luggage.
See, you don't have to check a bag anymore or pay extra because your bag was overweight, and this means the airline doesn't get the money, and THEY HATE THIS ONE WEIRD TRICK!
There's something unsettling about AI Angry People. They look demon-possessed.
But . . . if you're able to fit more into the suitcase by compressing the clothes, it doesn't follow that you'll avoid overweight charges. Aren't you more likely to get the overweight charges because you fit more stuff in the bag?
One of the evergreen approaches in this miserable shite: powerful forces don't want you to see this, know this, hope to suppress it, etc. Because we're all victims of these powerful forces. But these vendors are on your side. They're striking a blow for the common person, the Costco Shopper.
Have I used this one before? Look at these miserable people.
YOU WORKED
FOR DECADES
YOU DESERVE A QUALITY CROCKPOT
COSTCO HATES IT WHEN YOU USE THIS BENEFIT YOU DESERVE BECAUSE YOU WORKED
Concerning
our recent post on oddly specific AI music settings:
Lol

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Thursday.
item.description:
More work
in Sunderwood Park. Today they tore up all the reeds around the Slough of Despond.
Sunny, and - I know, I know - short-sleeved shirt weather.
Last day! Never happen again!
Rumors of rain and tornados all day, with a gloomy front pushing in at suppertime. Not a day of great emotional vigor - Wednesday and Saturday are the days I have to get through. It takes extra effort to work, move, produce, and such. But I do it.
So pin a medal on
me
, I guess.
On the way back from errands I stopped at Infinite Intoxicants to get some vermouth. To show you how unskilled I am in the ways of cocktails, I didn't know vermouth was perishable. I had a huge bottle I'd bought for some party, and was certain it had gone over. I paused at the Blended Whiskys section, and one of the ever-helpful clerks came over to see if I wanted to try something. Anything. Why yes. I
do
believe I can find something to try. Do you have a bottle of the 30-year Skye open?
Back up: year or two ago I noticed a new line of whisky on the shelves: Isle of Skye. It was offered, as they used to say, at Popular Prices. I tried a bottle, the entry level, was pleased, and added it to my rotation. Since then Iâve seen half a dozen other varieties come out. A special Cigar edition. A Smoky edition. A 17-year-old
intended to be sipped while studying the works of David Hume
edition. Thereâs a 30-year. Iâm always in awe of that sort of long game. Well, lads, letâs put it up and leave it, and come back in five years to start the 25 year old.
Who makes it? I asked. The clerk he looked it up, and thereâs only one distillery on the island, and itâs Tallisker, so Isle of Skye could be sourced to that venerable brand. Huh! Who knew.
Well, I looked it up, and it's produced by Ian Macleod, a Scottish company with many brands. The companyâs website says Ian Macleod himself started making Isle of Skye in 1933.
Juuuuuust maybe the clerk was trying to give it a cachet it didn't earn, to see a bottle? It's possible.
âThis is new,â I said to the clerk. Hedges and Butler. It has an intentionally cluttered label, suggesting an ancient pedigree. Lots of kings.
The address, EH52 5BU, comes back to Broxburn. Letâs go to the street view!
I would guess thatâs
Roberto
.
Anyway, I said it might be one of those venerable brands with a long history someone bought and revived, and the current product has nothing in common with the whiskey King George enjoyed. If there was a specific recipe, you canât guarantee that the distilleries that provided the various parts of the blend are still around, or if theyâve kept the ingredients the same. So yes, itâs been reformulated, and itâs now made by . . . Ian Macleod.
Iâll try some on my next trip. By the way, I was looking at some Isle of Sky locations, far up north, areas with no towns of any great size, and saw a church icon. Ah, let us look at some flinty old honest house of worship and tradition, keeping the ancient traditions alive on this sea-sprayed spit:
The reviews - and there are seven - say it is âa quiet place with no tourists.â
Another noted that the main thing to see was âcow hoof prints.â
It was built in 1810. Eventually there werenât enough people to maintain it, and it fell apart.
Anyway, I'm glad I noticed a new whisky, because now I'm thinking about that small ruin in an obscure part of Scotland, and wondering what happened. When the roof fell. When the walls toppled. What was the last hymn sung in that space? The last prayer?
This week's prompt. To tell you the truth, when I looked at the image in the folder, written and stored a year and a half ago, I wouldn't have been able to identify it without context.
I mean, it's just your basic demon, right?
No: it's as critical piece of popular culture history.
He SPOKE!
I didn't enjoy it all that much. I seem to remember it was a sloppy and uninvolving table. But another machine came along to the Valli shortly thereafter, and it was the greatest pinball machine of all time.
It has no equal. You might tout a machine that had some innovative feature like MagnaSave, but thatâs a nice gimmick. You might make the case for the original 8-Ball - it sold more tables than Deluxe, for some inexplicable reason - but youâd be wrong. Nothing had the combination of skill shots and options like this one. It, too, spoke.
Whoops;
beaucoup D'Anglais
But who was the voice? It wasnât a synthesized voice, was it? Apparently it was. Not a digitized snippet, but a robot encouraging us to Chalk Up, and chiding us when we used Too Much English.
What was the first pinball machine? Some say (citation needed; who?) itâs
Baffle Ball
, but it had no bumpers or flippers.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
item.description:
Last night I dreamt I went to Jasperwood again
.
Well actually no,
but I probably will tonight. Or rather this morning, since I go to bed after midnight. So tomorrow I will say "this morning I dreamed I went to Jasperwood again, but it was probably dark out when I was dreaming, so in away it was last night, inasmuch as the concept of 'night' is somewhat elastic, and depends on mood, the amount of light, whether you've gone to sleep or not, and so on." Anyway I'll work on that opening sentence, see what I can do.
POINT IS, I don't know where all my coats are, and which ones I gave away. Coats, parkas, jackets. I had about 16. Two winter parkas for the harshest days, for snowblowing duty. Many light spring / autumn jackets. different colors. She wanted me to do something about them long before the eviction, although I don't know if she demanded that I get rid of some. It was all a blur, anyway. Where would I go? Would there be room? Who knew? So I think I gave half of them to Goodwill. Now it's getting cold, and I have six jackets with the same weight.
This is why I cannot talk to her.
I should be able to walk to my closet in my house and get the proper coat. Thus I will dream tonight of walking up the steps to the front door and using my old key and turning left to open the doors of the beautiful hall closet and choose from a selection of coats I always took for granted.
I guess this was my problem. I always took my closet and my coats
for granted.
Stupid man.
The picture above is from Southdale, where I went to get a new jacket. That is the subject of Friday's column, because there was a moment that just stood up and waved a flag and said "Seven hundred words on this matter, no sweat." Southdale has now gone upscale, its latest overhaul. Looks nice, mostly full; not a lot of traffic. I used the loo on the lower level, the part that used to go to Al's Diner, and before that led to a subterranean concourse that certainly still exists, like walled-up catacombs. On the way I noticed something that made me sag a little bit, with sadness for the Bygone Things:
Looks like an 80s residue, but I believe it's from the 90s overhaul, back when the mall looked like this. (My photo.)
It's a style that aged out by decade's end, and everyone thought it looked weightless and gimcrack-baroque. Now it's the subject of sad nostalgic recollections on subreddits about malls and the 90s and
Global Village Coffeehouse aesthetics.
(This isn't GVC, but you know the bookstores and Starbucks abounded with the style.)
At least Southdale is still a going concern. I read today of a hotel in downtown Minneapolis that sold for, oh, $240 mil a while ago, and changed hands today for $5 million. Everyone in Minneapolis who owns a house will probably have to pay $4.27 to make up the lost tax revenue. I remember when it was built. It was a Radisson, so it was pretty good.
It was good to go to the Mall and walk around. Rainy day, perfect place. But like downtown Minneapolis, there is an emptiness in the soul of the place. Southdale doesn't have that dead-and-forgotten downtown feel, but it's lost something, too. It was once so much livelier, and useful. I suppose I should be grateful it's still here.
Now and then I am reminded that I live a few blocks from the old Howard Johnson where my family stayed on our first trip to the Cities in the early 60s, and I just think . . . it's a bit too on-the-nose. I can see an editor saying "okay, well, what point are you trying to make?"
I don't know!
"That you can't go home again, but you can be caught equidistant between totemic architectural constructs that define a lost sense of post-war confidence and enthusiasm?"
Yeah okay maybe
In between bouts of rain,
we ventured out to note the changes in the world. New this morn: Big dig at Sunderwood.
There's no heading into the field anymore.
After the gym, we went to the lake. The man-made one. Something was different, and I noticed it right away.
The fountain in the middle of the lake is off. No more spray, no more ripples. All is calm.
Oh, one more thing:
on the evening walk, we saw two of the local turkeys. I think they're the last survivors.
It's possible they were struck by a car and forcibly transmuted into one turkey, but it's probably just the angle. From now on I will call these guys Doh and Dal.
Okay, another thing.
CHALLENGE TIME. There are two sentences in this Bleat that explain this image.
Find them.
Itâs 1925.
I'll bet the womenfolk hated being a "Burley Lady."
Well, let's see how different things were, so many years ago:
Yes, we have been hearing this over and over and over, and itâs never true. Might have been a production issue, though.
The bright lights of Hollywood lure another lad from the farm:
IMDB does not record his name. Sounds like he wouldâve been an extra in some oaters, uncredited. But the folks back home would go to the theater in hopes of a glimpse.
Theyâre still arguing about war debt.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
item.description:
Rain all day. At point it faded to drizzle, so we went out to Sunderwood Park to do what needed to be done. Ah: machinery on the move, terraforming.
Overdid it at the gym, so my shoulder hurts. Home to a nap - ah, should check phone for messages. Daughter wondering about Pentagon infrastructure fortification effort. Ex has finally paid off the phone but cannot unlock phone. Sis-in-law passes along news about bomb threat at Daughterâs old high school.
So, checking messages before the nap was a mistake. But fell asleep anyway.
Made a wonderful supper with the leftovers sausage my own pasta sauce (as if thatâs difficult) and a ton of fresh basil. Sent a picture to Daughter as part of the ongoing reassurance effort: Dad is not eating gas station burritos in a parking lot while listening to country-western on the AM radio. Rain, so no walk. Off to work. I keep finding parts of the 2027 site updates that I havenât finished. There are so many things. Took a break to check the Misc folder to see if thereâs anything I was intending to discuss. . . . ah.
Okay, I know I'm rehashing - sort of - a topic I was banging on about yesterday. And to repeat: I am not against the existence or usage of AI, but I am driven mad every day by the profusion of krep.
The world does not have to be ugly and the world does not have to be fake It is our obligation to oppse both conditions.
So:
This guy.
I hate that my first reaction is to doubt his existence, and then I'm glad I do. I saw an ad for this book somewhere, and everything about it, I mean
everything
struck me as AI. Itâs off in ways you canât quite describe, beginning with the title of the damned thing.
I asked AI if it was AI, and AI said it was AI. Over at Reddit they were debating whether the YouTubes associated with the âauthorâ were AI, given the number of videos released in a short period of time, the factual inaccuracies, and my favorite - mispronunciation of things a robot wouldnât catch. No, route 128 isnât pronounced âone hundred and twenty eight.â
"His" youtube webshite has the style I have come to loath with murderous intensity:
An American Icon - but there's darkness beneath the matronly cheer, because everything you knew is false and everything was horrible and sad and she was probably SA'd! (Can't say the words you know)
What, did they go rogue and sew women's sleeves to the desk so she couldn't leave the house?
Cities! Heat-resistent glass! Nothing you thought was true! Everything was really REALLY
dark
underneath
but now you know and you're smarter than everyone else who doesn't know how DARK Pyrex was
Let me guess, she was based on a German sex doll? NO ONE KNEW THAT! NO ONE WAS READY FOR THAT!
Also, you'll note that everything is "most impossible."
They sold it to MOST WOMEN who were IMPOSSIBLE TRAPPED in SUBURBIA!
It goes on like that forever. Tons of hour-long videos released within days of each other.
I donât log in to YouTube all the time, so I see the basic stuff it presents to the general population. Same thumbnail format: AI lettering, some guy making a shocked face, a red arrow, and some words about something was DESTROYED or FAILED or was the WORST. Itâs an infinite buffet of salty chum with several purposes: accumulating money and time and eyeballs, of course, But the unifying theme is the broken and empty state of the world. There is no point to doing anything. Everything is lame. Everything
ages poorly
.
The only things you can do: REACT, or EAT.
The latter is a popular topic, as we saw yesterday. I have never in my life wanted to seek out a series of moving images of someone eating. I don't know why anyone would. As for the former: there are innumerable videos of people reacting to some cultural creation, as if the act of responding means anything or communicates anything. It doesn't. Oh, it might make people feel superior (I knew about that a year ago and did my own reacting) or B) provide "relatable content" so we can be Just Like Our YouTube Friend before turning on them in a year for a petty reason, or C) give people the chance to adopt the reaction as their own, relieving them of the need to experience the thing themselves.
You could say that movie reviews in print did the same thing, I suppose, but with a review you have to look at words and process them into a thought; the reaction videos are just watching people pull faces and nod and dribble phonemes.
Again,
obviously
I'm not the target market.
I did watch, start to finish, without glancing at my phone, the Drinker's latest video on the Narnia movie. Tell me if anything about these pictures stands out.
The shot below is controversial, since she's not supposed to be able to do things, and the name of the pub was where Tolkein and Lewis met, and she destroys it, but that's not what I'm pointing out.
I despair. It's beginning to seem as if THE COLOR will never go away. I've been banging on about this for
years
.
Tonight's ads on TV:
The world has a false and unnatural tone.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.
item.description:
For a week the mornings
have been cold, temps in the 40s - but then, after noon, the day thinks wait a minute, wait a minute, I can do better, and the warmth floods in on breezes that have none of autumnâs haughty chill. On Saturday it was in the 60s in the morning, and everything got brighter and hotter. Birch and I went to the lake and did the long walk, from which the image above was taken. Short sleeves again! Itâs a blessing. Itâs been a blessing all week, and we all knew this was the end.
True fall moved in around five and took the temps down ten degrees. Also around five the police showed up.
Okay, rewind. I was over at the Giant Swedeâs for a merry chili-fest that included the Crazy Uke and the entirety of his clever brood, and the Swedeâs kids were there as well, and a guest - like me, not related by blood or bonds. This was his first introduction to the particular verbal and intellectual and emotional pyrotechnics of the Swede-Uke Confluence, and itâs like tossing a match into a box of fireworks. Great fun. All the rituals were observed before the meal: a shot of vodka and the Lordâs Prayer, everyone in a circle, holding hands. Iâd brought Birch, and he decided that the group chant was the perfect time to start barking, and as we tried to drown him out by raising our volume, he barked louder. Adorable. Everyone there loves dogs, so thereâs that.
The police came because four Youts from down the street had walked through the alley, thought it would be fun to pick up a piece of wood that had a nasty 16â spike driven through it, and throw it over the Swedeâs garage. It bonked the Uke's daughter on the dome, and lucky for her - if you can put it like that - she wasnât speared with the rusty nail, so thereâs that.
It takes a certain type of sociopathy to pick that up and throw it towards the sound of people conversing and laughing.
The Giant Swedeâs ex-wife, to the surprise of no one, chased after them, but they lolâd and loped away. The police were called. Since no one could be found, no report was made because nothing happens in situations like this. They just keep their eyes peeled for four youths walking through alleys, and then let them pass because theyâre not spearing people with pieces of retaining wall
at the moment.
I had my chili outside on the patio in shirt sleeves, even though it was now in the minor 60s. Birch was more or less good, since there was food about and he could leverage his charisma to get some. At one point he barked in a way that indicated he was overloading, so I took him out across the street to walk and mark. Thereâs a classic mid-century structure, the sort of featureless building that nevertheless says elementary school. I am not quite certain why its most prominent vertical feature is an incinerator.
\
Talked to the new guy about movies, top faves, etc. He mentions he liked War of the Worlds, and had been terrified when he was it on video because he was, you know, ten. SIGH. I asked if heâd seen the original, and he didnât know there was one. I do not hold this against anyone. I have come to expect that even the brightest youths interesting in movie and arts do not have a cultural literacy that goes past 1978. The best and smartest have, at least, an understanding of the
shape
of things, and perhaps have seen the seminal films. They can talk about the studio system and the rise of the young directors in the 70s. But I find it hard to convince them to watch old movies. Old in my sense. Thereâs always something new and fun and shiny, and I understand: one watches the products of oneâs time. But thereâs so much that just languishes in the dark unwatched, and eventually its tropes and faces and sounds and styles ebb away into nothingness.
On the other hand, the odd cultural status of the 21st century - the way nothing really seems to change - means that
War of the Worlds,
the Spielberg version, doesnât seem dated at all, even though itâs (sigh) 21 years old. Even in 1977 the 1953 War seemed to be from another era.
The good news: there are people who love the old movies, and will use AI to make new 1940s noirs. And theyâll be interesting, because they will have directors who are making intentional choices. Someoneâs going to make the
Maltese Falcon
sequel. I mean,
the scriptâs right there.
Iâm not opposed to this.
BTW, the link has an image to another Falcon sequel, which Iâd forgotten about. Itâs supposed to be bad. It has Elisha Cook Jr. and Lee Patrick - the original movieâs secretary - reprising their role.
Take a look at the poster.
This was intended to make you think of . . .
This, of course.
But what was
The Sting poster
supposed to make you think of? (Bob, put your hand down, I know you know.)
It wasn't the norm for their cover design . . .
. . . , but they used it often enough that you could say it was part of the standard design.
I have in my head, for whatever reason, a
general
idea of magazine styles in the 20th century. I donât know what the modern analogue might be. Landing page designs? App icons? YouTube thumbnail styles?
Anyway, it was great fun,
and I drove home blasting good driving music. When we got to the parking garage I was again the realities of the Fred Demographic: Saturday night, and everyoneâs in. Everyone's sitting in boxes and ordering Doordash.
It was only 7, and we had the night ahead, me and Birch. I could work on things that didnât have to be put up tomorrow. I could do some design and watch a movie out of the corner of my eye on the second screen, a B&W World for Summer 2027. Only had to check email to see if Ex had made any progress on the Phone Situation, and lo: no. "The day had been crazy," no time.
No idea what crazy could possibly mean. Donât care.
(Period of conflicting emotions eventually cauterized with recollection of unkind and contemptuous remarks)
(Vague equilibrium achieved, but remnant curiosity and a need to ask: so. Was it worth it?
Everything better now?)

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Friday.
item.description:
I have another grocery-store ethical quandary. Not an ethical dilemma, thank heavens; those are gnarly. This is must a quandary. The problem has to do with Trader Joeâs fine olive-oil potato chips. At least 10% of the bag, perhaps more, looks like this:
So?
you say.
Itâs a potato chip
. Yes, but more like potato
chips
, fused together in a dense little tuber-slab. Theyâre not fun to eat. The dog loves them, but they provide too much gustatory information, in an unappealing way. Iâd like to take them back, but do I deserve an entire new bag?
Thereâs a big sign at TJâs with a drawing of an eagle, who is not the storeâs mascot. Or is he? Was he? There used to be signs that said a stuffed eagle was hidden around the store somewhere, and if a kid found it heâd get a sucker. I havenât seen that in years. The eagle persists. The sign says âTried it? Didnât like it? Get your money back.â The eagle looks a bit sheepish and is pulling out his pockets, holding greenbacks. I tried that once. I bought something and didnât like it and went to the customer service desk. A long-time manager Iâd seen there for years was absolutely uninterested and gruff, and his attitude seemed to be: didnât like it? And you want your money back? Really?
But I want to take these things back and show them. The bag is mostly empty. I fed the misfits to Birch, but when I found two thick chips towards the bottom I just said this is ridiculous. I cannot trust this bag. But do I deserve a whole new bag, just because I had an attitudinal shift? Thatâs the ethical quandary. Do I offer them up as an indication of a quality control issue, eschew compensation, and just do it so theyâll believe the next person who comes along? That would be paying it forward, to use a term I despise. Or perhaps Iâm the tenth person this week, and the manager will draft a letter tonight to the home office asking WHAT the HELL is going on with the Olive Oil Chips.
Or, I just give them to the dog.
It is two-column night,
to my surprise. Iâve been addle-pated all week about the date. I blame food. I decided last night to have these Chili-Lime chicken skewers for Thursday supper instead of the usual Thursday Fish, so I set them out to defrost the previous night. This somehow reset my calendar.
Well, it canât be Thursday, thereâs no fish for supper, therefore I donât have two pieces due tomorrow.
Actually, Iâve just been preoccupied. But not any more. I am sharp and in focus.
You know what I look forward to? Garbage night. Taking out the trash. It was always the Thursday post-supper duty in my old life, and it somehow signaled an important part of the week. Almost the weekend. Good things to come the next day. Iâd set them out and behold the hills of Jasperwood and the lights on in the house above, and sometimes spread my arms in pride and satisfaction. AND THUS IT WILL ALWAYS BE SO!
<fates_laughing.jpg>
What I do not miss is slipping on the ice taking out the bin and bringing it back, or being unable to drag it up the driveway because the footing was slick, and being stuck. Can't go forward. Sliding backwards, helpless.
Will I get a snowblower? Of course. There's the driveway to blow out. It would be amusing if I ended up with another corner lot, although 1/10th scale. I'll get Rooster grit, too. She banned that because it got tracked into the house.
Something small and compact, a home. A place to perfect. I'm looking forward to it and think about it every day and also am struck by how it seems so fucking
lonely
.
You're wondering

You may know the couple. Mr. & Mrs. Lavoisier. Scientists.
Consider their work:
Lavoisier is noted for his discovery of the role oxygen plays in combustion, opposing the prior phlogiston theory of combustion. He named oxygen (1778), recognizing it as an element, and also recognized hydrogen as an element (1783).
By using more precise measurements than previous experimenters, he confirmed the developing theory that, although matter in a closed system may change its form or shape, its mass always remains the same (now known as the law of conservation of mass), which led to the development of the balanced physical and chemical reaction equations that we still use today.
Lavoisier helped construct the metric system, wrote the first extensive list of elements, in which he predicted the existence of silicon, and helped to reform chemical nomenclature. (1787)
His wife and laboratory assistant, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, became a renowned chemist in her own right, and worked with him to develop the metric system of measurements.
Her individual bio's impressive, too.
Remarkable people. The intellectual vanguard of a sophisticated, inquisitive culture.But that culture changed with remarkable speed and ferocity.
At the height of the French Revolution, he was charged with tax fraud and selling adulterated tobacco and was guillotined despite appeals to spare his life in recognition of his contributions to science. A year and a half later, he was exonerated by the French government.

After the war, he returned to Hollywood, where he worked in both films, and later, in television. He was also the father of actress Elizabeth Montgomery.
Thatâs a life. But itâs the other fellow that matters today.
Thatâs Elliott Nugent. Heâd go on to have a successful and varied career as an actor, director, and writer. He directed Alan Ladd in the â49
Gatsby
, did a flick with Hope, and so on. He was the co-writer and director of
The Male Animal
, a Fonda / DeHavilland movie based on a play he wrote with Thurber. Iâve always said I thought Thurber was somewhat jealous of Nugent - they went way back to college, where Nugent stood up for a sickly unpopular poorly-dressed Thurber, and helped him gain social acceptance. Something tells me Thurber never forgave him for it.
Itâs entirely possible Iâm wrong; other sources say they remained close friends, especially at the end when their careers were on the downward path and both were drinking, a lot. But Nugent had that Hollywood glamor, and at his peak he must have swum with a fast, bright crowd. I think of Thurber as being an owlish loner sitting in the corner smoking and wishing someone would come up and tell him how wonderful he was.
Itâs just a suspicion but Iâve had it all my life, since I read a thick bio of Thurber.
Anyway: I have a connection to Nugent. Itâs as tangential as you can get. Itâs a three-degree-of-separation that leads to innumerable four-degree situations. Iâm four degrees away from the man who wrote
Casablanca
, Julius Epstein! Four degrees from Thurber, for that matter. Why?
Her co-star, Alan Bunce, was married to Nugentâs sister. I knew Peg in her last years, and of course she knew Bunceâs wife, and Iâm 100% certain she knew Elliott, or at least met him any number of times. So thereâs my three degrees. Via Nugent, my sixth-degree roster is absolutely star-studded.

now

Ike was eventually killed by a local deputy sheriff, and Phineas, after serving prison time for a stage robbery, moved to Globe, where he died of pneumonia and was buried in 1906.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
item.description:
EARLY AM
Woke without the usual enthusiasm. Sometimes on Tuesday I wake thinking of the things I set aside to make the day good, and they give me a smile. Today, nah. Meh morn. Open the shade: gray day. Check the temp: cold. The warm weather was gone for good, and I knew that yesterday. When we got back from the morning trip to fertilize the world I had this strange flashback, a mood of emptiness and solitude, something that had struck me sharp and hard when I was in London a year ago. Right before the letter. A sense of weary vacancy.
Went through the day as usual: work on the site in the AM, edit the Substack, do the art, then something new and different: I ironed lots of pants. O the excitement. Well, colder weather, best start dressing in good pants and nice sweaters, for some reason. Lunch was leftover pasta with the Trader Joe's hot Italian sausage, and they're not kidding: every bite a firecracker. Rather pointless. Gym, a quiet walk in Centennial, some comtemplative time in the chair by the lake, then the weekly big Target trip: get a bag of dog food and some chew sticks, can't run out of those. When I got home to the apartment in the late afternoon light, all cloudy outside the big windows, I felt that London feel again. Well! Nap. That always resets the day.
5:37 PM Sitting outside at the Yard,
which is the dog's yard of Yard, watching him work on the big log he dragged in from the field, studying the Grok responses to some necessary questions. Pretty much what I expected. A lot depends on the blood work, it seems.
I note that I have a badge for a missed call: it's the vet. He left a message. Says the blood work looks good, wants to talk about the sedation options I'd discussed. I'd missed the call because, at 4:35, Birch was seizing. This is absolutely horrible and unequivocably bad news, unspinnable, with only one resolution.
The MST, we were told, was 2 to 6 months with medication only. The upper range is 12 months, which is deemed "rare." We're at 11 months. That's if it's a brain mass. The next step, I expect, will be to put him back on Keppra - he went off that a few months ago at the vet's suggestion. The literature suggests that "many dogs regain useful control for months with a two-drug regimen." He had his old pep under the Keppra. If that doesn't work, then they'll suggest a higher dose of the phenobarbital, and/or another drug - which leads to lethargy.
If he can't summon the desire to go to the field or sniff the greenery at Centennial, what's the point?
I know, easy for me to say.
To clarify: I hadn't heard him seize, because we were napping. His sharp bark woke me up, and I was confused - he never does that. Usually rests on his dog bed and waits until I wake. Must be hungry. But he was preternaturally alert, and when I patted his head I felt dampness. Checked his bed: damn. Got him a Frosty Paws for focus, then put everything into the washing machine. He recovered quickly enough, and we went for a walk. Snapped him back into focus, dispelled the disorientation. When we got back I sat on the base of the light pole - again, to clarify, this was the second light pole base, farthest from the Fred; we go there sometimes so my cigar whiff wafts not into the common area. He has big sticks there as well. I'm thinking, I wish the blood work didn't look good, as far as absorption. Maybe it's an
absorption problem.
No, it's a brain tumor problem.
Spent the night doing nothing I can remember, except sorting and clipping and other things I can do with my mind off, or elsewhere. Poured a scotch at 10 and started looking at the websites I will, eventually, need to call.
Jasper was very old and slow, and slept most of the time.
Birch, I am certain, will be alert and engaged, and look at me to be sure it's all okay.
Do I have to take him down the elevator to let the vet in the building, because he'd be unhappy left alone?
Do I have to walk down the hall back to the apartment, watching his ears bounce as he trots back home?
Itâs 1959.
I'm guessing they were the only paper in town, and felt no competitive pressure to look interesting.
The sorrows of young Klaus:
This seems a bit suspicious, what with the first shot in the leg. But a subsequent story in another paper said he was despondent over breaking up with a local girl, so perhaps.
Apologies, but this was originally intended for July. Obviously.
You know youâre over the target when you start taking flag, as they say.
A related bit of patriotic encouragement on the editorial page:
QUEERY FOR THE OLDERS
The editorial page has a piece about THE FILTH. SMUT, as they used to call it.
It sounds as if the filth-peddlers or SMUT-MONGERS just mailed solicitations to everyone, which seems like a bad way to fly under the radar.
This might bear some investigating.
Mr. Amateau shows up first in LA papers in 1959 as the âchairman of membershipâ of the West Hollywood Optimists Club. Prior to that, the name shows up as the âOil Editorâ in a Louisiana paper, but I donât think thatâs him. The 1956 LA papers have an Albert J. Amateau giving a lecture at the Biltmore Hotel, titled âWhat you may be overlooking in the Iberian Peninsula,â delivered to the Foreign Trade Associationâs meeting. He was described as an âattorney and a sponsor of American Friends of Portugal,â and someone who âpioneered the production of American television and motion picture films in Portugal and Spain.â
But hold on. In another newspaper story about charges levied against the guys who helped this Amatreau, he's identified as âAlbert
A
. Amateau" in a few stories.
Searching ahead in 1961, I find this:
Two years to serve the 6-month term, then go back to the old job of being a foreign-affairs egghead? It's possible. OR, Al
J
. Amateau was
a legit local foreign-affairs guy,
and Al
A
. Amateau was someone different. But: Albert J. died in 1996 at the age of 106, so he would have been about 70 in 1959.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
item.description:
We've quite the melange today, but no high drama, and only one molar-grinding interlude of situational fury. Always the challenge: how to make this banal and solitary existence interesting? Let's begin.
Story of the day in a few images:
This was the largest log he's ever found in Sunderwood Park, and after this shot, he dragged it all the way back to the backup stick depository. Getting it over the fence wasn't easy, but he managed. Then we -
No, wait.
Went to Zork Storage to put away some things, and was somewhat vaguely intersested in this. The plastic over the 1 button is broken from use, the number is rubbed away by use. So . . .
Why 1, but not 2? Everyone who gets in the elevator goes to 2, otherwise they wouldn't be in the elevator. Is everyone angry when they're done, and they punch #1 extra hard? Experience has taught me that I'm angrier going up. I'm just disgusted going down. Is it the slowness of the controls that makes people punch it again because the doors have closed but the car hasn't begun to move?
In the afternoon, a visitor on the balcony:
That's a Nothern Paper Wasp. A look at
the wikipedia entry
is one of those portals into a world of ignorance both broad and specific:
P. fuscatus
is a part of the order Hymenoptera, the suborder Apocrita, the family of Vespidae, and the subfamily Polistinae, the second-largest subfamily within the Vespidae, of which all are social wasps. The Polistinae comprise four tribes, including Polistini, Epiponini, Mischocyttarini, and Ropalidiini.
It's like reading Plutarch, except with insects.
Now that you know the places and players, here's the story of a Monday. In the morning, out to the field in shorts, since the weather was still warm. Ran into TAD on the way out, no time to chat alas, off to a meeting. Or, I'm a tiresome chatterbox. I finished up the Substack, and we hit the road to make the 11 AM vet appointment.
To park in front of the clinic you have to approach going south, so I had to drive through my old neighborhood to get on Lyndale. Ever found yourself muttering all sorts of miserable curses because you don't live somewhere anymore? This was, and is, my favorite neighborhood in my life, anywhere. So I said some loud and bilious things about her in the privacy of my car. Yes, in front of the dog. For all I know he agrees. He perked up when we were driving through. His eyes brightened and his tail thumped.
Sorry, this isn't home anymore, just the place where someone drives a needle in your leg.
The vet moved next door a few years ago, leaving its old buidling empty. I spent many hours there, since I always took the dog to the vet as part of my long marital history of Doing Nothing. Birch needed a REBP, or Ruinously Expensivbe Blood Panel. This would check the effect of the phenobarbital on his liver and kidneys. My main question was . . . well,
and?
If the drugs that keep him from seizing are bad for the organs, then what? Supplements, I guess. They're also checking the pheno levels to test for efficacy, and again: well, he's not seizing, I think that might be our answer. A heartworm test is tolded into the REBP, so I guess I'm saving money.
He behaved well, al;though he aspirated so many treats while getting the draw he started hyperventilating and spitting out treat-chaff. The tech laughed, because it happens all the time. Afterwards we went to Sister-in-Law's place to chat, and that was nice. I picked up some boxes I'd left there when I started breaking down my office and off-loading the contents.They were the first I moved, a long time ago. I've no idea what's in them. One crate I could open - the hated matchbooks, which took up space in the
storage room
, of all places, the
gall
. Proof I was a hoarder. It was nothing anyone needed to have.
Gym. The walk to Centennial Lakes. Warm and bright, but with 7% more Fall than Saturday.
We couldn't tarry at the watering hole spot, as there was a couple in the chairs, deep into a serious conversation. He was holding her hand and talking low and she looked a bit shell-shocked.
Trader Joe's for just a few things, which of course ended up being twice as many things. I debated over the Pumpkin Butter, because I have several years of memories of unused Fig Butter and Pumpkin Butter in the fridge. But it's the fall! Shouldn't I pave my crumpet with Pumpkin Butter? It's not mandatory. You are permitted an crumpet unslathered with seasonal cliches.
I bought some ginger beer, because I intended to have a Moscow Mule in the evening. I've never had one. Vodka and ginger beer and lime. When I bought the ginger beer at Trader Joe I told the checkout clerk I was making a Moscow Mule tonight. She was middle / late-middle age but fit, long blonde hair, with this queen-of-the-roadhouse vibe, maybe. She said it was her dad's favorite drink.
"I don't have the copper mug, though," I said.
"You gotta have the copper mug! Go over to Total Wine, they'll have one."
"I don't think so! I was there for a pint glass for Guiness, and they didn't have it. You'd be surprised how little barware they have."
"World Market?"
"Same story. No pint glasses. Wine glasses galore but scant on cocktail glass."
"
No
."
"Yes. I know. What's the world coming to when you can't find a pint glass or a copper mug?" She was as dismayed as I was. I like her style.
Home. Troubled nap. Coffee on the balcony afterwards, where the wasp dropped in. We (Birch and I, not the wasp) took our walk
before
supper, the shape of things to come, what with early sunsets. When the sun went down it took all the warmth with it, closing up shop and putting the day's receipts in a safe.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
item.description:
Birch had another one. Itâs hard for me to discern the severity, since I donât know if I woke up in the middle, or the end. It was 2:45. Afterwards he was less disoriented than he used to be. I have a plan to get him focused: a Frosty Paws ice cream treat calms him down and puts him back in a familiar state of mind, it seems. He barked a bit but calmed down soon. We fell back asleep.
Woke to a gray day and a weary sad sense of inevitability, again. This is two in one month. One âbreakthroughâ per month is supposed to be okay. I thought,
well, itâs the end of the month, maybe we can count this as the October Seizure.
I did the laundry to clean the dog bed and the towels. We took a long walk in the morning and I let him roam all over the field to find
le spot juste
. My shoes were soaked when we got back and the day laid ahead like a cold dead thing.
It got better. But. But. As with the last time, my mind goes ahead to next month, the one after that - I see him here, still okay, and then I consider the possibility that he will not be here. IF IT IS A BRAIN TUMOR. They said it wasnât epilepsy. Okay. Unlikely. But itâs been almost eleven months. Mind races around that one, discarding evidence and denying probabilities and all that. Heâs not fine but he is. Every day, heâs my Birch, with all his moods and habits and pleasures. Every morning heâs happy to go out, tail up, his ears bouncing up and down as we trot down the hallway. Lifeâs good!
You have to remember that heâs a dog, and hence is taking things as they come. He looks forward to things, of course. He anticipates them. When we went to the Edina Spine he walked to the place where he likes to drink, only to find it drained. There was a little deflation you can see in his ears:
He went to all the spots, and they were all dry.
We walked on until we got to the lake, and there he had a sip. Back to the car, off on some errands. Back to the Fred, happy walk to the elevators, down the hall: it was that time of day when I had a few pieces of salami as a snack, and he would wait for a slice. Everything was good. After the nap it was warm enough to sit on the balcony with a cup of coffee, and of course he had to come out, nails clattering on the metal floor. After dinner we took our walk, and ran into the wild turkeys. They hadn't left, not yet. He enjoyed his usual sniffing spots and found some new fascinating thread that dragged him into the great field. Then we went to the Yard, which is the space - literally, a yard, 3' X 3' - where he keeps his sticks, and I finished my cigar and he toyed with a wet ripe log.
Horrid start and a perfect day.
It made me angry again, though. I do not like to be angry again. But it reminds me how I had told ETBF that he deserved to pass in his own backyard, his own home. (For that matter, so did I.) I suppose heâs lost the memory of that place. It plays no role in his life anymore. But it was his realm, his great big yard where he chased things and ran for sticks, and laid in the sun in the grass. Goddammit.
That's not the reason I don't want to have conversations with her, but it's one of them. Every subject has something burning in its core.
If he goes here, at the Fred, it will be horrible afterwards, empty and vacant. A lot of the brio I feel here will be gone. The
two-of-us-against-the-world
mood whenever we head out, and he looks up at me to make sure everythingâs jake, the little rituals of the day, the one-sided conversations - itâs miserable to imagine the loss.
It would be easier at The Last Place, the house I might buy, IF? I donât know. I love the view from Fred Base One, a lot; I like the conversations in the elevator, the liveliness of the place, the park right outside the door, the way the place is appointed. Maybe Iâll just stay. And then I think: that means
Here, and no further.
That just seems like THE END, with nothing of consequence to follow.
No, no, go get a house, and then . . . miss all the human society at the Fred.
Itâs been a long day. Iâm not tired. But Iâm tired.

She looked at me, nodded, and said âIâve seen them. Iâve seen them all my life.â
It was said in a way that would be appropriate if you were remarking that you had a long lifetime acquaintance with cheddar cheese, not apparitions that proved the existence of the afterlife, or at least some persistent spiritual manifestation. I did not exactly ask her to go on, but my expression mustâve encouraged her to relate the tales, and she started with the particularly annoying spirit that lived in the house with her three children. He had a habit of opening doors, and one time her littlest somehow got out of his cradle and went across the street. This was the fault of the spirit, which may have been a gypsy, rumored to have been buried in the area. At one point, she said, it got into bed with her, and I asked if it was just a presence or an actual manifestation or something she could see - and I was tempted to say âare you sure this just wasnât your husbandâ - she said she could see it, and she kicked it right out. thatâs it thatâs thatâs enough youâre out.

The second incident had to do with getting locked in a pub where she worked, and the owner had to come by with a key, the key didnât work in the lock. Not sure you can blame spooks for that. The ghost of the third example was in Wales, where she was living in some flats that have been knocked together, three of them, and each had their own staircase. The third staircase on the end, the circular staircase gave her such feelings of cold, frosty dread that she could not go up it. Oh, thatâs just old Jack and the lady.â There was a story about a drowned husband, a wife who refused to leave the flat, and all that.
After three stories, I was fascinated, but I also was hoping there was not a fourth since they did tend to go on. Iâll give her credit for this â years of telling the stories over the years had taught her to boil them down to the essential details. I thanked her for her tales and moved on.
